docs.title: How the course runs
docs.text:
Two teaching modules with the ⚙ AI-assisted/agentic-SE practice thread woven through both, then a flexible end-of-term block:

  • Module 1 (Weeks 1–8) — Foundations. Build a code language model: transformers, training, preferences, reasoning, RAG and agents, evaluation. Runs alongside Project 1 (build → use → break → assure your own code LM).
  • Module 2 (Weeks 9–11) — ML in Production. Requirements, architecture, quality assurance, operations, responsible engineering — for systems with LLM components.
  • Weeks 12–14. Midterm 2, advanced ⚙ topics from the current literature, then the Project 2 finish: draft → design presentations with preliminary results → final conference-format paper.

The full week-by-week schedule, grading, and policies are in the syllabus. Slide decks are posted on the slides page after each class.

docs.title: Reading List
docs.text:
A suggested reading list for this course — not a complete bibliography, and not everything the slides cite. It is mostly software engineering research, with the AI papers you need to make sense of it. Pick what your project needs.

For Project 2, the research radar (due Fri, Oct 2) asks for three papers you actually opened. Three from this page is a perfectly good answer.

Venues and years are given for convenience; check the canonical version before you cite anything.

docs.title: Start here — where the field is going
docs.text:
• Hassan et al., Agentic Software Engineering: Foundational Pillars and a Research Roadmap, arXiv:2509.06216 — the agenda the ⚙ thread follows; most sections end in an open question sized for a course project
  • Hassan et al., Towards AI-Native Software Engineering (SE 3.0), arXiv:2410.06107 — the shorter vision paper
  • Fan et al., Large Language Models for Software Engineering: Survey and Open Problems, ICSE-FoSE 2023 — the map of the whole area
  • Hou et al., Large Language Models for Software Engineering: A Systematic Literature Review, TOSEM 2024 — the exhaustive version; use it to find work near your topic

docs.title: Living collections
docs.text:
• AI Teammates in SE 3.0 — curated, continuously updated: https://github.com/SAILResearch/AI_Teammates_in_SE3
  • ICSE 2027 Competition Track — what the community thinks is worth competing on right now, and a possible venue for a strong artifact: https://conf.researchr.org/track/icse-2027/icse-2027-competition-track

docs.title: Code generation and how we evaluate it
docs.text:
• Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code, arXiv 2021 — Codex, HumanEval, and the definition of pass@k
  • Liu et al., Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? (EvalPlus), NeurIPS 2023 — weak tests inflate benchmark scores; the correction matters
  • Austin et al., Program Synthesis with Large Language Models (MBPP), arXiv 2021
  • Li et al., StarCoder: May the Source Be With You!, TMLR 2023 — what an open, documented code-model release looks like
  • Joel, Wu & Fard, A Survey on LLM-based Code Generation for Low-Resource and Domain-Specific Programming Languages, TOSEM 2025 — (instructor's work) where code LLMs stop working, and why
  • Wu & Fard, HumanEvalComm: Benchmarking the Communication Competence of Code Generation for LLMs and LLM Agent, TOSEM 2025 — (instructor's work) what happens when the problem description is ambiguous, inconsistent or incomplete, and whether the model asks

docs.title: Agents for software engineering
docs.text:
• Jimenez et al., SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?, ICLR 2024 — how agent progress is scored
  • Yang et al., SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering, NeurIPS 2024 — the interface is the design
  • Wang et al., OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents, ICLR 2025 — an open platform to experiment on

docs.title: AI-assisted development — the human evidence
docs.text:
• Peng et al., The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot, arXiv 2023 — the controlled experiment everyone cites
  • Barke et al., Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models, OOPSLA 2023 — acceleration vs. exploration; the best qualitative account
  • Vaithilingam et al., Expectation vs. Experience: Evaluating the Usability of Code Generation Tools, CHI EA 2022 — people like the tools even when they do not help
  • Perry et al., Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, CCS 2023
  • Pearce et al., Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions, IEEE S&P 2022 — the CWE-level security study; Project 2 topic B5 replicates its shape

docs.title: Testing, analysis and assurance
docs.text:
• Schäfer et al., An Empirical Evaluation of Using LLMs for Automated Unit Test Generation, TSE 2024
  • Lemieux et al., CODAMOSA: Escaping Coverage Plateaus in Test Generation with Pre-trained LLMs, ICSE 2023
  • Deng et al., Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Fuzzers (TitanFuzz), ISSTA 2023
  • Xia & Zhang, Keep the Conversation Going: Fixing 162 out of 337 Bugs for $0.42 Each Using ChatGPT, ISSTA 2024 — repair as a conversation, with the cost reported
  • Wu et al., Investigating the Efficacy of Large Language Models for Code Clone Detection, ICPC ERA 2024 — (instructor's work) an SE task LLMs are unexpectedly awkward at

docs.title: Engineering systems that contain a model
docs.text:
• Amershi et al., Software Engineering for Machine Learning: A Case Study, ICSE-SEIP 2019 — the nine-stage workflow and what makes ML different
  • Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems, NeurIPS 2015 — still the sharpest warning in the field
  • Wu, An Exploratory Study of V-Model in Building ML-Enabled Software: A Systems Engineering Perspective, CAIN 2024 — (instructor's work) what a classical process model does and does not survive
  • Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting, FAT* 2019 — Project 1's model card follows this
  • Gebru et al., Datasheets for Datasets, CACM 2021 — and Project 1's data sheet follows this

docs.title: Doing empirical SE research well
docs.text:
• Ralph et al., ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standards for Software Engineering Research — read the standard matching your study type before writing the proposal; reviewers will
  • Wohlin et al., Experimentation in Software Engineering (Springer) — the reference book for study design and threats to validity

docs.title: The AI side — enough to understand the above
docs.text:
• Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, NeurIPS 2017 — the architecture
  • Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3), NeurIPS 2020 — scale and in-context learning
  • Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla), NeurIPS 2022 — why your Project 1 model gets ~20 tokens per parameter
  • Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, ICLR 2022
  • Ouyang et al., Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT), NeurIPS 2022
  • Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization, NeurIPS 2023 — the simplification that stuck
  • Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models, NeurIPS 2022
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, NeurIPS 2020
  • Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, ICLR 2023 — the loop every agent runs
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning, 2025

docs.title: How to find more
docs.text:
1. Chase citations. Take one paper above, read what it cites and what cites it (Google Scholar's "cited by"). Two hops usually reaches the frontier.
  2. Skim recent proceedings — ICSE, FSE, ASE, MSR, EASE, AIware. The last two years are enough for this course.
  3. Mine the lectures. Every lecture closes on open questions, and any slide making a specific claim shows its source at the foot.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Generative AI — and large language models (LLMs) in particular — is materially changing how software is built. This course examines that change from both directions: software engineering of generative AI systems (building, evaluating, and operating systems with learned components) and software engineering with generative AI (AI-assisted and agentic development workflows).

AI-assisted and agentic software engineering is not a standalone unit at the end — it is a thread that runs through the whole course. From Week 1, students use AI coding assistants and agents as their required development workflow (and learn to validate their output); the foundations module explains how those tools work by building one; the production module covers how to engineer, evaluate, and operate LLM-powered and agentic systems. The second half of the course runs as a research seminar: students — solo or in pairs — carry out an original research project and write it up as a conference-format paper, which is submitted to a suitable venue after the semester ends.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Probability and statistics, linear algebra, data structures
  • Programming maturity (Python); prior exposure to machine learning is helpful but not required
  • Graduate standing, or instructor permission for undergraduates

docs.title: Undergraduate students
docs.text:
This is a graduate course, and a small number of undergraduates take it with instructor permission. They do the same lectures, the same Project 1, and the same exams. Three adjustments are recommended — suggestions, not requirements — so that the graduate-level research expectations land more gently on a student who has not been taught them yet:

Recommended adjustment Project 2 pairing Project 2 is done solo or in pairs; undergraduates are encouraged to pair with a graduate student rather than working solo. Design presentation Undergraduates paired with a graduate student may co-present the design presentation rather than presenting alone. Reading load One paper per week is a reasonable target where graduate students read two; the second is optional.

Everything else — Project 1 in full, both midterms, the findings table, the Week 8 pooled-findings session — is identical. Project 1 is deliberately scaffolded phase by phase and does not assume research experience, so it is the right entry point regardless of level.

The workshop-submission bonus is open to undergraduates on the same terms as everyone else.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

  1. Explain at a principled level how large language models are trained (pretraining, instruction tuning, RLHF/preference optimization) and how they generate output.
  2. Build, fine-tune, and evaluate a small code-generation language model end to end, including data preparation, tokenization, training, and benchmark evaluation.
  3. Analyze training datasets for provenance, bias, contamination, licensing, and governance implications.
  4. Explain embeddings as a representational framework and apply them to retrieval and similarity tasks (e.g., retrieval-augmented generation over codebases).
  5. Evaluate AI as a system component with defined cost, latency, reliability, safety, and privacy characteristics, and design systems that mitigate common failure modes (hallucination, adversarial inputs, miscalibration, prompt injection).
  6. Apply production ML practices — requirements, architecture, deployment, testing, monitoring, and MLOps — to systems with LLM components.
  7. Effectively use AI coding assistants and AI agents within a disciplined, collaborative development workflow (version control, code review, validation of AI-generated code), and design and evaluate agentic systems for SE tasks.
  8. Critically read and discuss current research in AI-assisted and agentic software engineering.
  9. Design and execute an empirical software engineering study involving generative AI, and communicate the results in a conference-quality research paper.

docs.title: Course Materials
docs.text: Two textbooks, used deeply — and no purchase is needed. The free materials listed below fully cover this course. T1 is a Manning book, but its companion repository (the complete, runnable code for every chapter) and the resources under it are enough on their own. If you are able and want to support T1's author — Sebastian Raschka, a former UW–Madison professor — buying the book is a fine way to do it. T2 is freely readable online, and every other reading is a research paper available via arXiv or the ACM/IEEE digital libraries (through the MTU library).

docs.title: Course Schedule
docs.text:
Two teaching modules with the ⚙ AI-assisted/agentic SE thread woven through both, then a flexible design-review block. Three 50-minute lectures per week (Mon/Wed/Fri) when there is no holiday. ×2 means a topic spans two sessions; ⚙ marks a practice session from the AI-assisted/agentic SE thread — supporting the projects, never examined. Slide PDFs are posted on the course website after each class.

Sessions are subject to change. The week-by-week content below is the plan, not a contract: pacing is adjusted to how the class is actually going, and current events in a fast-moving field sometimes earn a session. docs.title: Weeks 12–14 — Midterm 2, advanced topics, then the Project 2 finish
docs.text:
The end of the course runs: exam → advanced SE topics → draft → design presentation with preliminary results → final paper. The advanced-topic sessions are flexible — they are taught from the ⚙ deep-dive material and current papers, and any of them yields to a Project 2 clinic when teams need it.

Session Plan Mon, Nov 16 Midterm 2 review session Wed, Nov 18 Midterm 2 — covers the Module 2 decks, taught through Fri Nov 13 Fri, Nov 20 ⚙ Advanced topic 1 — agentic SE, the full deep dive ⛔ Nov 23 – 27 Thanksgiving — no classes Mon, Nov 30 ⚙ Advanced topic 2 — AI for testing and assurance, in depth Wed, Dec 2 ⚙ Advanced topic 3 — instructor's pick from the current literature, or by class vote Fri, Dec 4 Paper clinic · draft due (end of day) Mon, Dec 7 Design presentations + preliminary results, first block (8 min + 2 questions; five talks per session) Wed, Dec 9 Design presentations + preliminary results, second block Fri, Dec 11 Course wrap — the professional stance · final paper + artifact due

Why the advanced topics sit there. They are cutting-edge material — agents, AI-for-testing, whatever the literature is doing this month — taught when exams are over and students are deep in their own research. They sharpen Project 2 work in flight, and they seed next steps (and next-cohort topics). They are never examined.

Why the presentation comes after the draft. Presenting design plus preliminary results means every talk has substance, and the feedback — the questions and discussion in the room — arrives exactly one revision week before the final deadline, when teams can still act on it.

Not comfortable presenting your own idea? That is allowed for. If you would rather not share your novel idea publicly before submission, you may instead present one closely related paper, end to end — its problem, method, evidence, and limitations, plus one slide on how it connects to your project's area. Same slot, same length, same rubric; tell the instructor by the Fri Dec 4 draft deadline so the sessions can be ordered.

docs.title: Where the slack is — and is not
docs.text:
The semester has 40 class meetings (Fri Oct 30 is a deadline day, not a class): 23 in Module 1's weeks, 8 in Module 2's — two of them online — and 9 in the Weeks 12–14 finish block. The advanced-topic sessions (Nov 20 – Dec 2) are the slack: each one yields to a Project 2 clinic, an overflow presentation slot, or a snow-day catch-up before anything else moves. Everything before Week 12 is committed.

Presentations run five talks per 50-minute session (8 min + 2 questions), so Dec 7 and Dec 9 hold ten. With solo-or-pair teams a class of twenty can produce up to fifteen talks: talks 11–15 go to Wed Dec 2, whose advanced-topic slot converts to a third presentation session, and only past fifteen does the Fri Dec 4 clinic yield. The final Friday stays free for the wrap and the deadline.

A voluntary demo hour in finals week (Dec 14–18) remains available — this course has no final exam.

Each topic has more material prepared than its sessions allow; the slides are built to be selected from, not marched through.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Component Weight Midterm exam 1 (Module 1) 10% Midterm exam 2 (Module 2) 10% Participation & in-class engagement 10% Project 1 — Build it, use it, break it, assure it 25% Project 2 — Research project (conference submission) 45% Bonus — workshop submission (instructor-approved) +5%

There is no final exam. The two midterms are short, in-class exams: Midterm 1 covers the Module 1 foundations lectures taught through the Week 6 review (through reasoning — the Weeks 7–8 material on retrieval, agents and evaluation is not on it); Midterm 2 covers the Module 2 lectures. The ⚙ AI-assisted/agentic SE sessions are practice-oriented and are assessed through the projects, never on an exam. Each examinable lecture ends with a 'Key takeaways' slide; those slides are the examinable core.

Bonus credit (+5% of the course grade). A team whose final paper is reviewed and approved by the instructor submits it to a suitable conference workshop or similar venue (e.g., an ICSE/FSE workshop, AIware, or an MSR/EASE track — chosen with the instructor over the winter break; the realistic deadlines fall January–March) and earns bonus credit for every team member. The target is deliberately a workshop, not a top-tier main track — a workshop paper of up to 8 pages (not including references) is what one semester honestly produces, and a good workshop with engaged reviewers teaches more than a main-track rejection. The bonus is awarded for a completed, instructor-approved submission — not for acceptance, which is decided long after grades are due. Approval means the paper meets a real venue's bar: a falsifiable research question, a fair baseline, reported variance, an honest threats-to-validity section, and compliance with the venue's formatting and AI-disclosure rules. Teams that are not approved lose nothing; the bonus only ever adds.

docs.title: Participation & in-class engagement (10%)
docs.text:
• Sign in, and you have it. Attendance is the whole requirement — sign the sheet each class. There is no discussion quota and nobody keeps score of how often you speak.
  • Discussion is assumed, not graded: the paper discussions, the hands-on sessions, the pooled-findings session and the design-presentation Q&A are how this class runs, and everyone is expected to join in naturally.
  • One way to lose points: disrespect. Every student's questions, answers and presentations are treated with respect. Dismissing or belittling another student's contribution costs participation credit.

docs.title: Project 1 — Build It, Use It, Break It, Assure It (25%, individual, Weeks 1–9)
docs.text:
Full spec: the Project 1 page on the course website

The question Project 1 answers: how should software engineers be trained when AI is part of the process? The course's answer is that you make them build the component, use it for real work, attack it, and then engineer the checks that catch what they found.

One deadline: everything is due Fri, Oct 30 — one bundle: model card + repo, task report, findings table, QA report + a 3-minute recorded demo video, AI-use log + reflection. The four phases have a recommended pace, not graded deadlines:

Phase Recommended pace What you do Hand in (Oct 30) 1 · Build by Fri Sep 25 Train a small code model with nanoGPT, then one ablation — remove a part, predict the effect, measure it Model card (incl. ablation) + repo 2 · Use by Fri Oct 9 Use your own model on a real SE task, on 20 real inputs Task report 3 · Break by Fri Oct 16 Red-team it — find 10+ distinct failures Findings table 4 · Assure by Fri Oct 23 Build checks that catch them; measure your catch rate QA report + demo video

The pace exists because the later phases cannot be compressed into the last weekend — and because the Week 8 pooled-findings session (Fri, Oct 23) works from whatever findings table you bring that day. Everyone uses the same eight failure categories, so the class ends the term with a pooled catalogue of how a code model fails and how much of that ordinary testing catches; the final catalogue is assembled from the Oct 30 submissions.

The AI-assisted workflow is required, with a log and a one-page reflection.

Graded on what you found and what you built to catch it — not on model quality. A model that produces broken Python is fine; it gives you more to find in Phase 3. Rubric: the Project 1 rubric.

A note on data. Anonymised Phase 3 findings may be used in a study of how this course is taught. Participation is voluntary, opt-in via a Week 1 consent form, and has no bearing on grades in either direction.

Compute: the free GPU tiers (Kaggle, Colab and similar) are the working plan and are enough for this model; an ACCESS classroom allocation has been applied for and will be announced if granted — see the compute guide.

docs.title: Project 2 — Research Project with Conference Submission (45%, solo or in pairs, Weeks 3–14)
docs.text:
Full spec: the Project 2 page on the course website, with the proposal template, the suggested reading list, and the candidate venues.

An original research project on software engineering with/for generative AI, carried out solo or in pairs and written up as a conference-format paper. The goal is to take one question from idea to evidence to a paper an outside reviewer would take seriously — and then actually submit it. The rubric is the same for one student as for two; scope expectations scale with the number of hands, and the proposal is where scope is agreed. Undergraduates are encouraged to pair with a graduate student (see above — a suggestion, not a requirement).

The research thread starts in Week 3. Topics circulate on Fri, Sep 18, and by Fri, Oct 2 each student files a half-page research radar: solo-or-pair declared, two candidate directions, and three papers actually opened, one sentence each. The point is to put you in research mode early — reading the literature in September, while Project 1 is teaching you the craft. Your Phase 3 findings table will later sharpen the choice (revisit your radar after red-teaming — several of the best questions come from there). Full-time execution begins Nov 2, giving five working weeks before the draft. Many projects extend the Project 1 experience directly — four of the circulated candidate topics reuse the class's own models, probes, and QA checks.

Why we submit to a real venue. Writing for an external audience is the pedagogy, not a trophy hunt. A real deadline and real reviewers force the things this course is about: a question you can actually answer, an honest baseline, results you can defend, and limitations you state yourself. Teams that make it that far learn more than any term paper could teach.

How submission works — and what the target is. The target venue is a conference workshop (ICSE/FSE workshops, AIware, MSR/EASE tracks and similar), on purpose: a workshop paper of up to 8 pages (not including references) is the right-sized ambition for one semester, and setting that expectation up front is healthier than chasing a top-tier main track. Papers are submission-ready on Dec 11; teams may post an arXiv preprint then. Over the winter break the instructor works with each team to pick the workshop whose scope and deadline fit their work — options are discussed in Week 12, and the deadlines that suit a December finish fall between January and March. Papers the instructor reviews and approves are submitted for +5% bonus credit (see Grading).

Grading is independent of the outcome. Your grade reflects the quality of the research and the writing — the study you designed, the evidence you gathered, the honesty of your analysis. Acceptance decisions arrive months after grades are final and play no part in them. A rigorous negative result earns full marks.

Milestones (weights are of the Project 2 grade):

Date Milestone Weight Fri, Sep 18 Topics circulated (posted on the course website) — the research thread opens — Fri, Oct 2 Research radar — half a page: solo-or-pair, two candidate directions, three papers skimmed 5 Mon, Oct 26 Five-minute topic pitch, in class 5 Fri, Oct 30 Written proposal (problem, method, baseline, evaluation plan) — topic pivots allowed until Fri, Nov 20 15 Nov 2 – Dec 4 Execution — five working weeks; the ⚙ advanced sessions run alongside; check-ins in office hours — Fri, Dec 4 Full paper draft 15 Dec 7 / Dec 9 Design presentation + preliminary results 15 Fri, Dec 11 Final paper + artifact, submission-ready 45 after Instructor review over break → workshop chosen with each team; approved papers submitted +5% course bonus

docs.title: Use of AI tools
docs.text:
Using AI assistants (Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT, agents, etc.) is required for Project 1 and encouraged everywhere else — disciplined use of these tools is a learning outcome of this course. Requirements:

  • Disclose AI use in every deliverable (which tools, for what, and how outputs were validated); Project 1 additionally requires an AI-use log.
  • You are accountable for everything you submit: AI-generated code and text must be reviewed, tested, and understood. "The AI wrote it" is not a defense for plagiarized, incorrect, or insecure work.
  • AI tools are not permitted during the two midterm exams.
  • For Project 2, follow the target venue's policy on AI-generated text in submissions.

docs.title: Late work
docs.text: Project milestones lose 10% per day late (max 3 days) unless arranged in advance. The Dec 4 draft and Dec 11 final deadlines are firm because the presentation sessions and the submission timeline depend on them.

docs.title: Academic integrity
docs.text: All work is governed by the MTU Academic Integrity Policy. Collaboration within teams is expected; representing others' (or undisclosed AI) work as your own analysis is not.

docs.title: Accessibility and wellbeing
docs.text: MTU complies with the ADA and Section 504. Students with disabilities should contact Student Accessibility Services and the instructor early in the semester. Standard MTU syllabus statements (accessibility, non-discrimination, Title IX, mental health resources) apply and will be linked on Canvas.

docs.title: Project 1 — Build It, Use It, Break It, Assure It
docs.text: 25% of the course grade · Weeks 1–8 · Individual

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
How should software engineers be trained when AI is part of the process?

This course's answer is that you train them the way you train any engineer who works with a component they did not fully specify: make them build it, use it for real work, attack it, and then engineer the checks that catch what they found.

Project 1 is that answer, done. Four phases, one per idea.

docs.title: The four phases
docs.text:
Phase Weeks What you do What you hand in 1 · Build 1–4 Train a small code model with nanoGPT Model card + repo 2 · Use 5–6 Use your own model on a real SE task Task report 3 · Break 6–7 Red-team it — make it fail, on purpose Findings table 4 · Assure 8 Build checks that catch what you found QA report + demo video

One deadline: everything is due together on Fri, Oct 30. The week numbers above are the recommended pace, not graded deadlines — see One deadline below for why the pace still matters.

Each phase follows the lecture that supports it. You train after the training lectures, not before them; you red-team before the evaluation lecture, so that the lecture lands on something you have already felt.

Each phase has its own page below. Each ends with one deliverable and one question you should be able to answer out loud.

Companion reading. The course textbook T1 — Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) walks the same build in slow motion, with runnable code for every step (github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch). When a phase confuses you, the map is: tokenization and data loading → ch. 2 · attention → ch. 3 · the GPT architecture → ch. 4 · pretraining, loss curves and decoding → ch. 5 · fine-tuning → ch. 6–7. nanoGPT is the same model with the scaffolding stripped away.

The Phase 3 findings table is the one artifact the whole class shares. Everyone uses the same categories, so the class ends up with a pooled catalogue of how a code model fails and what catches it. Week 8 is a class session on that pooled catalogue — you will see what twenty people found, together, before anyone tells you what to conclude.

docs.title: Phase 1 · Build (Weeks 1–4)
docs.text:
Train a small code language model from scratch with nanoGPT.

Data. A prepared corpus is provided — permissively-licensed Python, deduplicated, already split by repository. Use it; assembling a corpus is not what this phase is teaching.

You still have to understand it: the data sheet asks you to say where it came from, what deduplication removed, and why the split is by repository rather than by file. Read the prep script; it is short.

Optional: build your own corpus instead. Say so in your data sheet and report what changed. This is genuinely more work, and it earns no extra marks — do it because you want to, not because you think you should.

Model. Use this configuration. It is small on purpose: it trains in a few GPU-hours and it is big enough to learn real structure.

Setting Value Layers / heads / embedding 6 / 6 / 384 Context length 512 tokens Tokenizer BPE, vocabulary 8192, trained on your training split only Training tokens about 20 × parameter count Precision bf16 if your GPU supports it

The ablation — learn what a part is for. Once your baseline trains, pick one modification from the menu, retrain, and compare:

Ablation What it teaches Remove the position embeddings why order information has to be injected 1 attention head instead of 6 what multiple heads buy 3 layers instead of 6 what depth buys Remove LayerNorm why training stability needs it — expect drama Context 256 instead of 512 what a longer window is worth on code Character-level tokenizer instead of BPE what a tokenizer actually does

Before the second run, write down your prediction — what will the loss do, and what will the samples look like? Then report, in the model card: what you removed, what you predicted, what actually happened (final validation loss for both runs, plus one side-by-side sample). Being wrong in your prediction is fine; noticing how you were wrong is the point.

One ablation is required; more are welcome if your GPU budget allows — each is one more training run. Different students will pick different rows, so the Week 8 pooled session also assembles a class-wide picture of which parts of a transformer matter most.

Done when: your loss curve falls and flattens, the model generates Python that mostly looks like Python, and your ablation comparison is in the card.

Hand in: your repository (data prep, training config, a README that reproduces your run) and a model card (template) — including the ablation section.

Be able to answer: why does a repository-level split matter, and what would a file-level split have done to your numbers?

If your training fails and time runs out, ask for the instructor's checkpoint. You lose the Phase 1 marks you did not earn and you keep Phases 2–4, which are 70% of the grade and where most of the learning is. Ask in Week 4, not Week 7.

docs.title: Phase 2 · Use (Weeks 5–6)
docs.text:
Use your model — not a commercial one — for a real software engineering task.

Pick one:

  1. Code completion — complete function bodies from their signature
  2. Docstring generation — write docstrings for undocumented functions
  3. Test stubs — generate test skeletons for existing functions
  4. Commit messages — draft messages from diffs

Run it on 20 real inputs taken from a repository you know well. Your own code from another course is ideal, because you can judge the output.

For each of the 20, record: what you gave it, what it produced, and whether you would accept, edit, or reject that output.

Hand in: a task report (template) with your accept / edit / reject counts and three examples — your best, your worst, and the one that was most nearly right.

Be able to answer: what is your model actually useful for, and where did it waste your time?

docs.title: Phase 3 · Break (Weeks 6–7)
docs.text:
Now try to make it fail. This is the phase that answers the course's question, so it carries the most weight.

Find at least 10 distinct failures. Not ten copies of one failure — ten different ways of going wrong.

Ways in, to get you started:

  • Give it code that is close to something it saw in training
  • Give it an unusual style, an unfamiliar library, a rare construct
  • Ask for something with a security-sensitive shape (path handling, subprocess, SQL, deserialisation)
  • Put a misleading comment above the function
  • Give it a function name that contradicts what the function does
  • Feed it non-English identifiers, or very long inputs

Log every finding in the shared findings table (CSV template, column guide), using the fixed category list. The categories matter: they are what make the class's findings poolable.

Category Meaning syntax The output does not parse invented-api Calls a function, method or module that does not exist wrong-logic Parses and runs, but does the wrong thing insecure Introduces a security weakness memorised Reproduces training data nearly verbatim prompt-sensitive A trivial rewording flips the answer context-ignored Ignores something clearly present in the input other Anything else — describe it

Hand in: the findings table, plus a one-page summary of the three failures you consider most serious and why.

Be able to answer: which failures would a test suite catch, and which would sail straight through it?

docs.title: Phase 4 · Assure (Week 8)
docs.text:
You found the problems. Now build the checks that catch them.

Pick three findings from Phase 3 — ideally three different categories — and build an automated check for each. Cheap and certain beats clever:

Finding A check that catches it syntax ast.parse on every generation invented-api Resolve every import and attribute against the real environment insecure A static analysis or lint rule for that weakness class memorised Substring match against your training corpus wrong-logic A test — and notice how much harder this one is

Then measure it. Run your checks across all your Phase 3 findings and report: what fraction does your QA catch?

That number is the point of the whole project. It is almost never 100%, and the gap is the honest answer to "how much can automated assurance actually do here."

Hand in: a QA report (template) with your catch rate, your checks as working code in the repo, and a 3-minute recorded demo video: run your checks live, show one failure being caught, show one getting through.

Be able to answer: which of your failures can no automated check catch, and what would you do about those in a real team?

docs.title: Also required, throughout
docs.text:
Build all of this using an AI coding assistant, and keep a log of it (AI-use log template): what you asked for, what you accepted, what you had to fix, and what it got confidently wrong. One page of reflection at the end.

This is not compliance paperwork. You are training a model and being trained by working with one — the log is where you notice the second thing happening.

docs.title: One deadline
docs.text:
Everything is due Friday, Oct 30 (end of day) — one bundle: model card + repo, task report, findings table, QA report + demo video, AI-use log + reflection. There is no class that day; the deadline is the session.

The phases have a recommended pace, not graded deadlines:

Pace Date What should be done Week 4, Fri Sep 25 Phase 1: model trained, model card drafted Week 6, Fri Oct 9 Phase 2: task report drafted Week 7, Fri Oct 16 Phase 3: findings table filling up Week 8, Fri Oct 23 Phase 4: checks running — and the pooled-findings session

Why the pace matters even though only Oct 30 is graded:

  • The later phases cannot be compressed. Breaking a model well takes evenings of poking, and Phase 4 needs Phase 3's findings. Students who start Phase 3 in the last week hand in thin tables — every year, in every course shaped like this.
  • The Week 8 pooled session (Fri, Oct 23) uses whatever table you bring. Come with ten findings and you compare against the class; come with two and you mostly watch. The final pooled catalogue is assembled from the Oct 30 submissions.
  • Midterm 1 (Wed, Oct 7) sits between Phases 2 and 3 — the pace gives you the exam week back.

If you are behind the pace at any point, say so in office hours — that is what the fallback checkpoint exists for. Ask in Week 4, not Week 9.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
See the rubric. One line: you are graded on what you found and what you built to catch it, not on how good your model is.

A model that produces broken Python is completely fine — it gives you more to find in Phase 3. A student who finds 15 real failures and catches 8 of them has done better work than one with a nicer loss curve and a thin Phase 3.

docs.title: A note on your data
docs.text:
Your Phase 3 findings table may be used, together with the rest of the class's, in a research paper about how this course is taught.

  • It is voluntary. Say no and nothing changes — same deliverables, same grade, no reason needed.
  • It is not part of your grade in either direction.

You will get a short consent form in Week 1. That is the whole of it; you do not need to think about it again.

docs.title: Compute
docs.text: See the compute guide. The working plan is the free GPU tiers — Kaggle and Colab are enough for this model, ablation included. An ACCESS classroom allocation is under review and will be announced if it lands. Run something trivial in Week 1 to check your setup works — do not discover a problem in Week 3.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Everything you hand in has a template on this site:

  • Model card and data sheet — Phase 1
  • Task report — Phase 2
  • Findings table — CSV, with its column guide — Phase 3
  • QA report — Phase 4
  • AI-use log — throughout

Grading is defined in the rubric; GPUs in the compute guide.

docs.title: Compute for Project 1
docs.text: Only Phase 1 (training) needs a GPU — Phases 2–4 run on a laptop. Budget ≈ 15 GPU-hours for the semester: a successful run takes 2–6 hours on a free-tier T4, you need two (baseline + your ablation), and the first attempt always dies on something — a path, a shape mismatch, an out-of-memory.

docs.title: Where the compute comes from — free tiers, today
docs.text:
Explore the free GPU resources first — they are genuinely enough for this model:

  • Kaggle Notebooks — a free weekly GPU quota (around 30 hours/week on T4/P100-class GPUs; check your account page for the current number). That alone covers the baseline, the ablation, and several failed runs. Save checkpoints as Kaggle Datasets so nothing is lost between sessions.
  • Google Colab (free) — a T4 with session limits. Checkpoint to Drive every few hundred steps so a disconnect costs minutes, not the run. Colab Pro (with an education discount where available) buys longer sessions and faster GPUs — a convenience, never a requirement.
  • A GPU you already own — a gaming laptop or desktop trains this model overnight.

Whatever you use, do the same three things: pin your environment, checkpoint regularly, and log training to a file (you will want the loss curve later).

docs.title: ACCESS — applied for, pending
docs.text:
An ACCESS Classroom (Explore) allocation (with the NAIRR Pilot education call as a complement) has been applied for and is under review. If it is granted, accounts and instructions will be announced on the course website, and you can move mid-project — your checkpoints and configs transfer. Nothing in Phase 1 waits on it: the free tiers are the working plan.

If compute fails you anyway, ask for the instructor's spare checkpoint (see the spec). No student's grade depends on any allocation working.

docs.title: Project 1 — Rubric
docs.text:
25% of the course grade. One row per phase. Marked out of 100.

Phase Marks Full marks means 1 · Build 25 Model trained to the given config. Loss curve falls. One ablation run with prediction written before the run and an honest predicted-vs-measured comparison. Model card complete, including why the split is by repository. Repo reproduces both runs. 2 · Use 20 20 real inputs, judged honestly. Accept/edit/reject counts reported. Three examples, including the near-miss. 3 · Break 30 10+ distinct failures, correct categories, specific why_wrong. caught_by_test_suite answered honestly. 4 · Assure 20 Three working checks. Catch rate measured over all findings. Clear account of what got through and why it is hard. Demo video shows the checks running. AI-use log 5 Honest, including what the assistant got wrong.

docs.title: What is not graded
docs.text:
• Model quality. Broken Python is fine. It gives you more to find in Phase 3.
  • Your catch rate. 40% honestly measured beats 90% claimed.
  • Whether the class paper is accepted anywhere.

docs.title: What loses marks
docs.text:
• Fewer than 10 findings, or ten variations of one finding
  • Categories used loosely — the class data depends on them being consistent
  • Anything after the one deadline (Fri, Oct 30) — the late-work policy applies to the whole bundle
  • A Phase 4 catch rate reported without showing what got through
  • An AI-use log in which the assistant never made a mistake

docs.title: The honesty premium
docs.text:
Marks are available for catching your own mistakes. "My first split was by file; here is how I noticed and what it did to my numbers" scores better than a clean number with no story.

This is deliberate. In Week 5 you study reward hacking; a rubric that graded only the number would be doing exactly what those lectures warn against.

docs.title: AI-Use Log — Project 1
docs.text:
Required. One row per meaningful interaction; a session of small completions can be one row. Aim for honesty and specificity over volume.

Date Tool What you asked for What you accepted What you had to fix Verified how

docs.title: The rows that matter most
docs.text:
Add these explicitly — they are the ones the reflection needs and the ones people skip:

  • It was confidently wrong. What did the assistant assert that was false? Invented API, wrong idiom, plausible-but-broken logic. How did you catch it?
  • It saved you real time. What would have taken an hour and took ten minutes?
  • You accepted something you did not fully understand. Everyone does this. Which was it, and what happened later?
  • You were faster without it. If that happened, say where.

docs.title: One-page reflection
docs.text:
Submitted with the log. Address, in your own words:

  1. Where did AI assistance genuinely help in this project, and where did it not?
  2. Give one concrete case of it being confidently wrong. What was the failure, and what caught it — a test, a type error, a review, or luck?
  3. Did you understand your own pipeline less well in the places you leaned on it hardest? Be honest; the answer is often yes and that is worth knowing.
  4. What will you do differently in Project 2?

Length is not the point. Four honest paragraphs beat two vague pages.

Your log and reflection may be used in the class paper only with your consent, and consent has no effect on your grade. See ../../research/seet-paper.md.

docs.title:
Data Sheet —

Follows the shape of Gebru et al., Datasheets for Datasets, CACM 2021.
Motivation
docs.text: What is this corpus for, and who assembled it?

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
• Source(s) and how files were selected
  • File count and token count, before and after each filtering step
  • Languages; Python version distribution if you know it
  • Licences present, and how you filtered for permissive ones

docs.title: Collection
docs.text:
• How and when it was collected; the exact snapshot or commit
  • Anything excluded, and why

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
• Cleaning steps in order
  • Deduplication: method (exact / near), and how many files it removed
  • Tokenizer: algorithm, vocabulary size, what it was trained on

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
• Train / validation / test sizes
  • Split unit — repository or file. Phase 1 requires repository. If you used file, say so, and say what you think it did to your numbers.
  • How you verified no repository appears in two splits

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• What this corpus supports, and what it should not be used for
  • Known contamination risk against the evaluation benchmark, and how you checked

docs.title: Distribution and maintenance
docs.text:
• Is the corpus redistributable under its licences? If not, ship the recipe that rebuilds it rather than the data
  • Who maintains it, and for how long

docs.title:
Model Card —

Follows the shape of Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting, FAT* 2019.
Model details
docs.text:
• Author, date, version
  • Architecture: nanoGPT decoder-only, N layers / N heads / D embedding
  • Parameters (excluding embeddings), context length, vocabulary size
  • Training seed · nanoGPT commit · your repo commit

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text:
• Intended: a teaching artifact for studying small code language models
  • Not intended: any use where the generated code runs unreviewed

docs.title: Training data
docs.text:
• Source, licences, token count, deduplication, split unit
  • Point at your data sheet rather than repeating it

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
• pass@1, pass@10, held-out loss, compression, syntactic validity
  • Benchmark used, problems, samples per problem, decoding settings

docs.title: Ablation
docs.text:
• What you removed or changed, and the exact config delta
  • Your prediction, written before the run
  • Final validation loss: baseline vs. ablated · one side-by-side sample
  • What surprised you

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Be specific and concrete. At this scale, expect at least: - Plausible code that does not parse — give your measured rate - Invented APIs and imports - Memorised fragments of training data (say whether you checked) - Python only; nothing about behaviour in other languages transfers

docs.title: Ethical and licensing considerations
docs.text:
• Licences in the training corpus, and what that implies for the output
  • Whether you checked for secrets or personal data in the corpus, and how

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text: What you would want a reader to know that the numbers do not show.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Task Report
docs.text: Name: · Task chosen: completion / docstrings / test stubs / commit messages Source of inputs: which repository, and why you can judge its output

docs.title: Results over 20 inputs
docs.text:
Count Accept as-is Accept after editing Reject

One sentence on what "accept" meant to you — you are the judge here, so say what you were judging.

docs.title: Best
docs.text: Input · output · why it was good.

docs.title: Worst
docs.text: Input · output · what went wrong.

docs.title: Most nearly right
docs.text: The one that looked right and was not, or needed one small fix. Usually the most informative of the three.

docs.title: Two questions
docs.text:
1. What is your model actually useful for? Be concrete and be modest — it has ~10M parameters.
  2. Where did it waste your time? Cases where checking the output cost more than writing the code yourself. Note these; they are Phase 3 leads.

One to two pages. Prose, not bullet fragments.

docs.title: How to fill in the findings table
docs.text:
The findings-table CSV — one row per distinct failure. Minimum 10 rows. Row 1 is a worked example; delete it or keep it, it does not matter.

Open it in a spreadsheet if you prefer. Submit it as CSV.

docs.title: The columns
docs.text: Column What goes in it finding_id 1, 2, 3 … category One of the eight below. Exact spelling — this is what makes the class data poolable what_you_gave_it The prompt or input, short what_it_produced The output, or the relevant part why_wrong One sentence. Be specific: "no such function" beats "bad output" severity low · medium · high — your judgement, one word how_found What you were trying when it broke caught_by_test_suite yes · no — would an ordinary unit test have caught this?

docs.title: The eight categories
docs.text:
syntax             output does not parse
invented-api       calls something that does not exist
wrong-logic        parses and runs, does the wrong thing
insecure           introduces a security weakness
memorised          reproduces training data nearly verbatim
prompt-sensitive   trivial rewording flips the answer
context-ignored    ignores something clearly present in the input
other              describe it in why_wrong

Use other sparingly. If you use it more than twice, you have probably found a category we are missing — say so, that is a genuinely useful contribution.

docs.title: The column that matters most
docs.text:
caught_by_test_suite. Everyone assumes tests catch model failures. Your table is the evidence for how far that is actually true, and it is the number the class discussion in Week 6 is built on.

Answer it honestly. A no is more interesting than a yes.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Quality Assurance Report
docs.text: Name:

docs.title: The three checks you built
docs.text:
# Catches which category How it works Where in the repo 1 2 3

Keep "how it works" to one sentence each. The code is the real answer.

docs.title: The catch rate
docs.text:
Run your checks over all your Phase 3 findings.

Count Findings from Phase 3 Caught by your checks Catch rate %

docs.title: What got through
docs.text:
List the findings none of your checks caught. For each, one line on why it is hard.

This is the most important section of the report. A catch rate below 100% is expected — what matters is whether you understand which failures resist automation, and why.

docs.title: Two questions
docs.text:
1. Which of your failures could no automated check catch? What would you do about those in a real team — and what does that imply about the review step?
  2. What would you build next, with another week?

docs.title: Demo video
docs.text:
Three minutes, recorded (screen capture is fine, no editing needed): run your checks, show one failure being caught, show one getting through. Include the link or file in your Oct 30 bundle.

Two to three pages plus working code in the repo.

docs.title: Project 2 — Research Project and Paper
docs.text: 45% of the course grade · Solo or in pairs · Research thread from Week 3 (topics out Fri Sep 18) → final paper Fri Dec 11

docs.title: What you do
docs.text:
Answer one research question about generative AI in software engineering, and write it up as a workshop-length conference paper — up to 8 pages, not counting references.

The paper is submission-ready on 11 December. Instructor-approved papers are submitted to a suitable conference workshop (ICSE/FSE workshops, AIware, MSR/EASE tracks — chosen together over the winter break) for +5% bonus credit. The workshop target is deliberate: it is what one semester honestly produces, and a good workshop with engaged reviewers beats a main-track rejection.

Project 1 gave you a protocol to run. Project 2 asks whether you can write one.

docs.title: The research area
docs.text:
Your project lives where this course lives, seen through two lenses:

  • AI-assisted SE research — studying what AI does to software engineering: code LLMs and their failure modes, agents and AI teammates, assistants and the humans using them. This is the subject of your study.
  • AI-assisted empirical SE research — running the study itself the AI-assisted way: AI helps you build the harness, mine the data, and draft the analysis, and your paper honestly reports what the AI did and how you verified it. This is the method of your study. You practice what you investigate.

Every candidate topic fits the first lens; the second is expected of all of them (it is also this course's AI-use policy applied to research). The course reading list maps the area — mostly SE research, plus the living AI Teammates in SE 3.0 collection and the ICSE 2027 competition track as views of the frontier.

Team size: one or two students. The rubric is identical either way — scope expectations scale with the number of hands, and the proposal is where scope is agreed. Undergraduates are encouraged — not required — to pair with a graduate student. "Team" below means you, or you and your partner.

docs.title: The five steps
docs.text:
Step Weeks What you produce 0 · Radar 3–5 Topics out Fri Sep 18; research radar due Fri Oct 2 — solo/pair, two directions, three papers 1 · Question 5–9 Sharpen one direction into a claim; five-minute pitch Mon Oct 26 2 · Plan 9 A proposal, due Fri Oct 30: method, baseline, what would prove you wrong 3 · Run 10–13 The experiments — five working weeks, Nov 2 – Dec 4, with the ⚙ advanced-topic sessions alongside 4 · Write & present 13–14 Draft (Fri Dec 4) → design presentation with preliminary results (Dec 7/9) → final paper (Fri Dec 11)

There is one formal presentation, and it comes after the draft. You present your design and your preliminary results — so every talk has substance — and the feedback you get — the questions and the discussion in the room — arrives exactly one revision week before the final deadline, when you can still act on it.

docs.title: Step 0 · Radar (Weeks 3–5)
docs.text:
Get into research mode early — reading, not committing.

Fri, Sep 18: ten candidate topics — each a claim with a method and a baseline — circulate on the candidate-topics page (released Fri, Oct 9). Every lecture also ends on an open question, and those are deliberately project-sized.

Due Fri, Oct 2 — the research radar. Half a page, graded lightly (5% of the project): solo or pair (and with whom) · two candidate directions that interest you · three papers you actually opened, one sentence each on what the paper claims and what it leaves open. That is all. The radar is not a commitment — it is proof you have started reading.

Why so early: reading the literature takes calendar time, not effort spikes. A student who has skimmed six abstracts by October pitches a sharper question in ten minutes than one who starts fresh in Week 9.

docs.title: Step 1 · Question (Weeks 5–9)
docs.text:
Sharpen one radar direction into a claim worth seven weeks.

Your Phase 3 findings table is the sharpening stone. Red-teaming your own model (Weeks 6–7) is where many of the best questions come from — revisit your radar after it and expect at least one direction to change. That is normal and free.

The test any question must pass:

Can you state a claim in one sentence, that could turn out to be false, and test it with the compute and weeks you actually have?

The commonest failure is a question that would be excellent with a year and a cluster.

Mon, Oct 26: five-minute pitch to the class. Question, why it matters, how you would test it.

docs.title: Step 2 · Plan (Week 9)
docs.text:
Write the proposal using the proposal template. Two to three pages.

The section that matters most is "what would prove you wrong." If nothing would, you do not yet have a research question — you have a demo.

Due Friday of Week 9 (Oct 30) — four days after the pitch, so the class's questions are still fresh when you write it. You have been circling this topic since your radar in September; the proposal is the write-up of a decision, not the start of one. (Oct 30 is also Project 1's deadline — both were finished work by then; the Friday is for assembly, not creation.)

docs.title: Step 3 · Run (Weeks 10–13)
docs.text:
Do the work — five working weeks, Nov 2 to Dec 4. Three things to know:

  • The ⚙ advanced-topic sessions run alongside (Nov 20 – Dec 2): agentic SE and AI-for-assurance in depth, plus current papers. They are there to sharpen your project in flight, and any of them converts to a clinic when teams need one. Office-hours check-ins are your checkpoints.
  • The proposal is your contract — with one escape hatch. Until Fri Nov 20, a team may re-scope or even replace its claim with instructor approval: one conversation, no penalty. The advanced sessions sometimes reveal a better question than the one you picked; that is what the window is for. After Nov 20 the claim is fixed — a scope cut is always allowed, but a late pivot cannot produce a Dec 4 draft.
  • One rule, from the ⚙ thread: write your evaluation section before you finish the experiments. It routinely reveals that the experiment you planned cannot support the claim you wanted, and mid-November is a much better time to learn that than December.

docs.title: Step 4 · Write (Weeks 13–14)
docs.text:
• Fri Dec 4 (end of day): full draft due
  • Mon Dec 7 & Wed Dec 9, in class: design presentation + preliminary results — 8 minutes + 2 of questions. Present the claim, the design, what the data shows so far, and what you will fix before Friday. Every student in the audience is a discussant — questions are expected; discussion is how the class runs
  • Not comfortable presenting your own idea? Allowed for. If you would rather not share your novel idea publicly before submission, present one closely related paper, end to end instead — its problem, method, evidence, and limitations, plus one slide on how it connects to your project's area. Same slot, same length, same rubric. Tell the instructor by Fri Dec 4
  • Fri Dec 11: final paper + artifact. The week between draft and final is the revision window — the questions from your talk, and the instructor's written feedback on your draft, are the input to it

docs.title: What a passing paper has
docs.text:
Not a template — the six things reviewers look for and first papers usually lack:

  1. A one-sentence claim that could be false
  2. A baseline you might lose to. A comparison you were guaranteed to win proves nothing
  3. Variance reported. One run is an anecdote — Project 1 should have made that vivid
  4. Seeds and decoding settings stated. Results nobody can reproduce cannot be believed
  5. Honest threats to validity. Naming your own weakest point before a reviewer does is the strongest move available to a student paper
  6. Contamination addressed, if you use a public benchmark. Not solved — addressed

docs.title: Deliverables and weights
docs.text:
Due Deliverable Weight Fri, Oct 2 Research radar — solo/pair, two directions, three papers 5 Mon, Oct 26 Topic pitch 5 Fri, Oct 30 Proposal 15 Fri, Dec 4 Full draft 15 Dec 7 / Dec 9 Design presentation + preliminary results 15 Fri, Dec 11 Final paper + artifact 45

Weights are of the Project 2 grade.

docs.title: Using AI tools
docs.text:
Encouraged. Two rules:

  • Disclose what you used and for what, in the paper
  • Follow the venue's policy on AI-generated text — read it before you write

You are accountable for every claim regardless of what drafted it. A fabricated citation is a fabricated citation.

docs.title: Project 2 Proposal
docs.text:
Author(s): one or two names · Date: · Working title:

Two to three pages. Prose, not bullet fragments — if you cannot write it as prose you do not yet have a project.

Write it to be lifted. Sections 1–5 of this proposal are your paper's introduction and method section, version zero. On this timeline (about twenty working days of execution), a team that writes the proposal well has two pages of the paper done on Oct 30; a team that treats it as paperwork writes those pages twice.

docs.title: 1. The claim (one sentence)
docs.text:
State what you believe, in a form that could turn out to be false.

Weak: "We will investigate LLM test generation." Strong: "Tests generated from a specification catch more injected faults than tests generated from the implementation, on the same functions."

docs.title: 2. Why it matters
docs.text: Who changes what they do if you are right? Two or three sentences.

docs.title: 3. What is already known
docs.text: Four to eight papers, and what each one leaves open. This section is where supervisors find out whether the project is real. If everything you cite says your question is answered, you need a different question.

docs.title: 4. Method
docs.text:
• What you will build or run
  • The dataset or benchmark, and why that one
  • The baseline — and be honest about whether you might lose to it
  • Independent and dependent variables; what is held fixed
  • How many runs, and how you will report variance

docs.title: 5. How you will know
docs.text:
• The metric, and why it measures the claim rather than a convenient proxy
  • What result would make you wrong. If nothing would, this is not yet research
  • How contamination is handled, if a public benchmark is involved

docs.title: 6. Feasibility
docs.text:
• Compute you need and where it comes from
  • The week-by-week plan to Week 14
  • The riskiest assumption, and what you do if it fails. Every proposal has one; naming it is not weakness

docs.title: 7. Threats you can already see
docs.text: You will not have solved these. Name them anyway.

docs.title: 8. Team
docs.text: Who does what. Two to three people, and everyone contributes to the writing.
